record.title: OpenAI, Google and Microsoft announce support for a shared robots.txt AI-training preference
record.summary: On 30 October 2026, OpenAI and Google announced plans to honor a shared robots.txt signal for website operators to express preferences about using content for generative-AI training. Microsoft also announced support and says its shared training preference will begin taking effect as it crawls from 1 February 2027. The mechanism is described in an individual IETF Internet-Draft, which is not endorsed by IETF and has no formal standing in its standards process. No live implementation, cross-provider conformance, or change in content collection or training data has been observed.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: On 30 October 2026, OpenAI and Google announced plans to honor a shared robots.txt AI-training preference; Microsoft also announced support and says its preference will begin taking effect as it crawls from 1 February 2027.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The cited individual draft defines the __usage_ai-training policy token in ordinary robots.txt groups, allowing path-specific preferences about use for generative-AI training while leaving existing crawler rules unchanged.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The IETF Datatracker identifies the document as an active individual Internet-Draft and says it is not endorsed by IETF and has no formal standing in the IETF standards process; Google and Microsoft both describe standardization work as continuing.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected sources do not establish live implementation or conformance across providers, legal enforceability, publisher outcomes, or changes to content collection or training data.

evidence_gaps.description: OpenAI, Google and Microsoft announced future support with different timelines; no live crawler behavior or conformance test has been observed. Microsoft says it will honor settings as it crawls from 1 February 2027.
The cited token definition remains an individual Internet-Draft without IETF endorsement or formal standards-process standing; Google and Microsoft say working-group standardization continues.
No evidence links these commitments to changes in crawling, content inclusion, training datasets, grounding use, publisher traffic, or other publisher outcomes.

brief.importance_rationale: If multiple major providers implement a shared training-preference mechanism, publishers could communicate one content-use preference across services instead of maintaining separate provider rules, changing practical web-data governance. The score is capped at notable because current evidence is provider announcements and an individual draft; implementations, conformance, publisher outcomes, and training-data effects remain unobserved.
limitations: The mechanism is specified in an individual Internet-Draft; the IETF Datatracker says it is not endorsed by IETF and has no formal standing in the standards process.

OpenAI says implementation is planned in the coming months; Google targets support in 2027; Microsoft says the preference begins taking effect as it crawls from 1 February 2027. These announcements are not observed implementations.
Microsoft separately announced page-level training and grounding controls; these product-specific controls are not the same as the shared robots.txt preference.
The policy token communicates a usage preference, not a crawling directive. No legal enforceability, provider conformance, changed data use, or publisher outcome was established.

Microsoft also announced support and says its shared training preference will begin taking effect as it crawls from 1 February 2027. The mechanism is described in an individual IETF Internet-Draft, which is not endorsed by IETF and has no formal standing in its standards process. technical.claimed_result: OpenAI and Google announced future support for the shared training-preference signal; Microsoft says it will honor the preference as it crawls from 1 February 2027. Microsoft also described separate page-level controls for training and grounding. No implementation or conformance has been observed.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official OpenAI, Google Search Central, and Microsoft Bing posts demonstrate that all three announced support or plans for the shared training preference. The IETF Datatracker establishes the current document’s individual-draft status and the draft describes the token semantics.
technical.implementation_status: Not yet demonstrated. OpenAI says implementation is planned in the coming months; Google targets 2027; Microsoft states its preferences begin taking effect as it crawls from 1 February 2027. This review found announcements and guidance, not observed crawler behavior.
technical.mechanism: The individual draft defines a robots.txt policy-token group—User-Agent: __usage_ai-training—to express an allow/disallow preference for generative-AI training on matched paths. It adds no robots.txt directive syntax and leaves existing crawler rules intact. Microsoft additionally describes page-level training and grounding preferences specific to its services; those are separate from the shared signal. The draft says the token is a use preference, not a crawling directive.
technical.regime: Website operators expressing preferences for generative-AI training through a shared robots.txt policy token; announced future support by OpenAI, Google and Microsoft, based on primary sources dated 30 October 2026. No live provider behavior was tested.
technical.reproducibility: The source text and draft are publicly inspectable; no implementation artifact or behavior was available to reproduce.
technical.strongest_baseline: OpenAI and Google describe separate provider-specific rules as the prior publisher burden. Microsoft adds that its own page-level grounding choices remain distinct. No measured baseline for publisher effort, provider conformance, or outcomes was inspected.

brief.title: OpenAI, Google and Microsoft announce support for a shared robots.txt AI-training preference
brief.why_it_matters: If implemented as announced, a shared preference could reduce the need for website operators to maintain separate training-use rules for each participating provider. Microsoft says training and grounding choices are separate; it warns that restricting grounding reduces visibility in AI-generated experiences, while neither choice guarantees inclusion, traffic, or payment. This exposes a potential discoverability trade-off for publishers, but no measured traffic or revenue effect is available. Microsoft has stated a 1 February 2027 start as pages are crawled, while OpenAI and Google give broader future timelines. These are provider commitments, not evidence of present compliance, legal enforceability, or changed data practices.
